prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1, the incretin effect and the biologically active form of the hormone, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep B041 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but the round-1 exchange has made me state more precisely why. The prize is for a discovery chain: Holst established the incretin effect and GLP-1 action in humans, Drucker defined proglucagon-derived peptide biology and the actions that made a therapy rational, and Mojsov's contribution is the chemical characterization of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide. I rest her inclusion on that peptide work and not on first discovery of the hormone, which is the framing Sandberg asked for. The resulting benefit is established, not projected: independent randomized trials show glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal effects. The citation names discovery, and the drug class follows from it.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still credit. Mojsov's priority is disputed with the Habener group, who are not on the supplied list, and the supplied record cannot settle that. The three-name limit leaves out Knudsen, whose protraction chemistry produced liraglutide and semaglutide, so the prize could be read as honouring the biology and not the medicine. Svenningsson and Wahren-Herlenius are right that the two strands are different achievements, and a trio cannot do both without strain. I hold my choice with moderate confidence, and the strongest argument against it is that a contested priority claim is a poor foundation for a third slot.

responses.point: The native peptide's short half-life was the obstacle, so the drug-development step, not peptide identification, is what turned the hormone into a therapy and deserves the third place.
responses.response: This is the argument that has moved me most, and I accept that Knudsen's work was the step that removed the obstacle to clinical use. I still think the prize tradition favours the discovery that makes a therapy conceivable over the engineering that follows. A rational long-acting analogue also depended on knowing which peptide form was active, and that is the part Mojsov supplies. Your test for me is whether her contribution was necessary and not one of several parallel ones. The supplied record does not show that cleanly, and I will not claim it does. That is why I describe my confidence as moderate, and why I would accept the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen configuration over losing B041 to a priority dispute.

responses.point: Agreement on the trio is not evidence that the priority question is resolved, and the committee should state that Mojsov's inclusion rests on peptide chemistry and characterization, not first discovery, and test it against the primary literature.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation and case_for to match. I now rest her inclusion on characterization of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and not on first discovery, and I do not treat our shared trio as confirmation. I cannot test the claim against the primary literature at this stage. The supplied summary does not show whether her contribution was independent of Habener's, so the uncertainty stays open in my statement. If the committee cannot document independence, my own standard says the third name should move to Knudsen.

responses.point: Without Knudsen's design work the physiology would remain a mechanistic finding with modest clinical consequence, and Perlmann would reconsider if Mojsov's contribution were shown to be decisive and independent of Habener's.
responses.response: I agree that the physiology alone did not reach patients, but I do not think the discovery would have stayed modest. The incretin effect, the active peptide and the rationale for long-acting agonists were established before the analogues, and they are what made the analogues worth building. We are both conditioning our third name on the same unresolved fact, Mojsov's independence from Habener. The difference is the default if it stays unresolved. You would default to Knudsen, and I would too, though I would want the citation to say plainly that we are honouring the therapy strand then. Your concern about newer cardiovascular, renal and neurological indications is fair, and I would keep the citation to diabetes and obesity.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps CAR-T as first alternative but not as a second prize part, citing the missing Eshhar, overlap with the earlier checkpoint recognition and the lack of solid-tumour efficacy.
responses.response: We agree that B035 should not be a second part this year, and I think your solid-tumour point is a better reason than mine. CAR-T works well in B-cell malignancies, and a citation would have to say so. That is the same kind of scope limit that Eshhar's absence is for the credit. I also agree no second part is justified, since all six of us proposed a single-part prize and a second part would take names from the three B041 slots. Where I differ slightly is that I would still rank B035 above B004 as a fallback, because B004's paradigm is already largely absorbed and recognized, as Svenningsson and Sandberg both note.

responses.point: The physiology and the drug design are both necessary parts of the chain, so Holst and Drucker for the physiology with Knudsen for the drug design describes the achievement faithfully within three names.
responses.response: I agree both parts are necessary, and your trio is internally coherent. What I do not accept is that necessity settles who takes the third slot, since active-peptide identification was also necessary. You say Knudsen's acylation was a creative solution and not routine development, and I find that persuasive on the science. It does not by itself outweigh the discovery strand for me. I also note that your configuration needs a citation covering physiology and translation, and a reader could say that merges two achievements. Mine has the narrower problem of one contested name.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's characterization of GLP-1(7-36) was independent of and necessary beyond the Habener group's work, which the supplied record does not establish and which would decide my third name.
Whether the committee wants the discovery strand or the drug-development strand honoured in one citation, since the two lead to different third names.
Whether the absence of Habener makes any B041 configuration too incomplete to defend publicly.
Whether B035 can stand as a fallback without Eshhar and given its limited efficacy outside haematological cancers.
Long-term safety of incretin therapies is still being defined.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure and no specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My documented co-authorship (eight works with Sandberg, per a count I have not audited), my spatial transcriptomics work and my shared KI affiliation with other members do not involve any credited name on the shortlist. I do not infer personal ties from shared institutions or topics, and I propose no recusal.
